implementation_notes: tenacity turns retry into a decorator assembled from three policies: a stop condition (stop_after_attempt, stop_after_delay, or a | combination), a wait strategy (wait_fixed, wait_random, wait_exponential(multiplier, min, max), wait_random_exponential, or sums such as wait_fixed(3) + wait_random(0, 2) for jitter) and a retry predicate (retry_if_exception_type, retry_if_result, retry_if_exception_message, combinable with |). When the budget is spent it raises RetryError wrapping the last exception unless reraise=True, and @retry decorates coroutines and context managers as well as functions, so the classic while-loop with time.sleep disappears from the call site. A hand-written loop stays reasonable for a one-off script, but the library's own defaults are unsafe - a bare @retry retries forever with no delay - so stop and wait must be set explicitly.
code_sketch:
@retry(
    stop=stop_after_attempt(4),
    wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=0.5, max=10),   # backoff + jitter
    retry=retry_if_exception_type((ConnectionError, TimeoutError)),
    reraise=True,
)
def fetch(url: str) -> dict: ...
pitfalls: A bare @retry retries forever with no delay - the library default is the unbounded loop, so stop and wait are mandatory.
RetryError hides the real exception in the middle of the traceback; reraise=True or e.last_attempt.exception() is needed to see the cause.
The decorator wraps the whole function, so side effects before the failing line run again on every attempt; retrying a function that holds an open transaction or mutates shared state is not safe.
wait_* strategies sleep with time.sleep (or asyncio.sleep for coroutines) and are not cancellable externally unless the stop condition includes a deadline.

variants.name: urllib3 Retry configuration on a PoolManager / requests HTTPAdapter
variants.idiom_name: urllib3.util.Retry(total, connect, read, status, backoff_factor, allowed_methods)
variants.implementation_notes: At the transport level retry is a configuration object: urllib3.util.Retry carries separate budgets for connect, read, redirect and status failures (plus an overall total), a backoff_factor that doubles the sleep per previous retry with backoff_max and backoff_jitter, a status_forcelist of codes to force retries on, respect_retry_after_header for 429/503, and allowed_methods which defaults to the idempotent verbs only - the library encodes the safety rule that a POST is not retried unless you say so. Attach it to a PoolManager (or to requests through HTTPAdapter(max_retries=...)) and every request through that pool inherits the policy, while the call site stays a plain request; exhaustion raises MaxRetryError wrapping the cause. Prefer this when the retryable unit is HTTP transport behaviour - connect resets, read timeouts, 503s - rather than application logic.
variants.code_sketch:
retries = urllib3.util.Retry(
    total=4, connect=2, read=2, status=3, status_forcelist=[429, 503],
    allowed_methods=frozenset(["GET", "HEAD"]),      # never retry POST here
    backoff_factor=0.5, backoff_max=10, respect_retry_after_header=True,
)
http = urllib3.PoolManager(retries=retries)
resp = http.request("GET", url)
pitfalls: read and other retries can re-send a request whose body was already consumed; urllib3 documents that these failures may have side effects, so the safe default (idempotent verbs only) must not be widened casually.
Errors are wrapped in MaxRetryError (requests re-wraps that in its own RetryError), so unwrap the cause before classifying it.
backoff_factor defaults to 0, which retries with no delay at all; set a factor and a backoff_max, and remember the sleep happens on the calling thread.
Each attempt internally creates an updated copy of the Retry object, so mutating a shared instance to change policy mid-flight is the wrong lever - configure it once.
